list.listitem: Mushroom poisoning produces a multitude of toxidromes depending on the mushroom species ingested. C

The first and best indicators of hepatic damage are an elevated AST, ALT, lactate dehydrogenase (LDH), and serum bilirubin. Glucose, fibrinogen, and prothrombin time are the best markers for hepatocellular failure. C
Identifying the time to symptom onset can help determine the mushroom toxidrome, guide medical management, and assist with defining prognosis. C
Longitudinal data from the American Association of Poison Control Centers suggest that only 50% of all patients with mushroom poisoning will develop symptoms and 30% will require treatment. C
The mortality rate with Amanita mushroom poisoning is 10 to 40%, but can be reduced to less than 5% with appropriate early intensive care. C
For amatoxin poisoning, based on case series consider N-acetylcysteine, silibinin, and penicillin. C

background.definition: Mushroom poisoning, or mycetismus, is a set of clinical toxidromes ranging from acute, self-limited gastroenteritis to hepatorenal failure and death depending on the species and quantity of mushroom ingested.

list.listitem: American Association of Poison Control Centers (AAPCC) data suggests 0.3% of poisonous exposures involved mushrooms.
The vast majority of cases of mushroom poisoning are accidental. However, fewer cases may be due to suicide attempts or ingestion of mushrooms purported to be hallucinogenic.25
Approximately 100 of the known species of fungi are poisonous. Some mushrooms have switched classifications from edible to toxic.

Approximately 6000 mushroom exposures were reported to the AAPCC in 2018. Of these, 3008 exposures (52%) were in children 5 years old and younger. Also, of these exposures, 1349 exposures (23%) were in adults 20 years old and older. Ten percent of calls were exposures involving hallucinogenic mushrooms (Psilocygin and Psilocin). Approximately 76% involved unknown mushrooms.

Actual incidence is uncertain: mushroom poisoning is a nonreportable illness; healthcare providers may diagnostically code mushroom poisoning sequelae, not mushroom poisoning itself; mild symptoms of mushroom poisoning are often not reported. However, it is advisable to report any/all cases of mushroom poisoning to the local Poison Control Center.
The AAPCC and Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC) often report regional clusters of mushroom poisoning.
The incidence of mushroom poisoning incidence is increasing due to greater demands for gourmet or hallucinogenic mushrooms.
Mushroom poisoning is most common during mushroom harvesting season, June through October.

There are 100,000 known species of fungi, with hundreds of new species discovered each year. Over 90% of mushroom-associated fatalities are secondary to the consumption of Amanita phalloides mushrooms.
In addition, new species of nephrotoxic mushrooms have recently been identified.26
In more than 90% of mushroom poisoning cases, the specific toxin group is never identified, and in more than 95% of cases, the causative species remains unidentified.
Mushrooms absorb heavy metals and pollutants from their environment, more avidly than other food crops. These include : arsenic, cadmium, mercury and lead, among others.
Mushroom poisonings may result from the misidentification of mushrooms during mushroom harvesting.
Mushroom toxicity, especially Amanita, can lead to fulminant hepatic failure.

Clinical symptoms and severity of mushroom poisoning depend on the mushroom species, amount consumed (amount of toxin delivered), part of the mushroom consumed, the geographic region where mushrooms were grown, and processing/preparation method.
Mushroom processing (boiling, cooking, freezing, etc.) may not alter the toxicity of the mushroom. Additionally, many edible mushrooms may cause GI toxicity if improperly stored.
The highest levels of amatoxin and phallotoxin are found in the mushroom gill; the lowest toxin levels are contained in the volva (see ).

Cyclopeptides are toxins that most commonly cause mushroom poisoning syndromes.
Two major groups of mushroom cyclopeptides are amatoxins and phallotoxins; phallotoxins are not absorbed in the intestine and cause negligible human poiosning. Amatoxin (alpha-, beta-, and gamma-amantinins) are notorious for causing the clinical symptoms of mushroom poisoning. Cyclopeptide poisoning has four consecutive stages: Latent Stage lasts 6 to 24 hours following ingestion and is asymptomatic; Gastrointestinal Stage lasts 12 to 24 hours and is characterized by intense abdominal pain, nausea, vomiting, and/or diarrhea; Convalescence Stage lasts 12 to 24 hours and patient appears to be improving; Final Stage begins 2 to 4 days after ingestion and lasts 4 to 7 days. Transaminases increase significantly, indicating hepatocyte damage and potential acute liver failure or multiforgan failure. Amatoxin mechanism of action: Amatoxins are taken up by hepatocytes, inhibiting protein synthesis and causing cell necrosis results. This process also occurs in the intestinal mucosal cells during amatoxin transport, causing gastroenteritis.
Mushroom poisoning severity correlates with presentation timing (time to onset of first symptoms).
Mushroom poisoning syndromes are stratified by presentation timing and target organ toxicity.
Early onset toxicity (<6 hr following ingestion) is associated with milder poisoning and recovery. Symptoms include gastrointestinal, allergic, and neurologic syndromes.

Late onset toxicity (6-24 hr following ingestion) is associated with more severe hepatotoxic (fulminant liver failure), nephrotoxic, and erythromelalgic (maldistribution of blood to hands and feet, so that these areas become red and warm to the touch) syndromes.
Delayed onset toxicity (>1 day after ingestion) includes most delayed nephrotoxic, neurotoxic, and rhabdomyolytic syndromes.

Mushroom poisoning can be prevented by avoiding consumption of wild foraged mushrooms and hallucinogenic mushrooms, as well as by preventing accidental mushroom ingestion by young children.Parents should educate children not to eat any mushrooms, unless shown to, and approved by an adult. C
In more than 90% of mushroom poisoning cases, the specific toxin group is never identified, and in more than 95% of cases, the causative species remains unidentified. C
The first and best indicators of hepatic damage are an elevated AST, ALT, LDH, and serum bilirubin. C
The best indicators of hepatocellular failure are glucose, fibrinogen, and prothrombin time. These labs should be monitored closely if liver damage from mushroom poisoning is documented. C

Differential.Differential_Name: Cholecystitis, acute appendicitis, peptic ulcer disease, peritonitis, acute ulcerative colitis

list.listitem: Mushroom poisoning produces several different toxidromes depending on the mushroom species ingested.
The most common mushroom poisoning syndrome results in GI toxicity, occurring within 3 hours of ingestion and resolving within 6 to 24 hours.

However, mushroom poisoning can present with a wide range of symptoms, but many species cause non-specific GI complaints initially. Consider mushroom poisoning in cases of GI toxicity, hepatic and renal toxicity, or mental status changes.

Key questions include: (1) time from ingestion to symptom onset (); (2) initial and current symptoms; (3) quantity ingested; (4) number of species were ingested; (5) source of mushrooms (location with pesticides or fertilizers); (6) processing and storage (refrigerated, cooked, boiled); (7) illness in others; and (8) alcohol consumption within 48 hours (disulfiram-like reaction with coprinus mushrooms).
Establishing time to symptom onset is crucial for guiding the diagnostic workup. See and for additional guidance.
Consider hallucinogenic mushroom ingestion when other substance abuse has occurred.
Mydriasis is present in more than 90% of patients with hallucinogenic mushroom ingestion.

Assess for anticholinergic symptoms (mydriasis, dry skin and mucous membranes, urinary retention, decreased bowel sounds, tachycardia, hypertension) and cholinergic/muscarinic symptoms (miosis, lacrimation, salivation, diaphoresis, urination, emesis, bronchospasm, muscle spasm, bradycardia). Also assess for altered mental status, weakness, somnolence, dysphoria, anxiety, agitation, respiratory distress, and jaundice.
Cardiac toxicity including acute heart failure, ventricular tachycardia, and myocarditis have been reported and can be fatal following Amanita, Tricholoma and Russula ingestions.

For all mushroom ingestions, check basic metabolic profile (sodium, potassium, chloride, carbon dioxide, creatine, BUN, and glucose), hepatic panel, and CBC. This is especially important for patients with diarrhea, vomiting, or severe gastroenteritis as these processes can lead to electrolyte imbalances. An initial hepatic panel establishes baseline liver function.

The first and best indicators of hepatic damage are an elevated AST, ALT, LDH, and serum bilirubin. Liver enzymes peak between 60-72 hours after ingestion. Recall that even in the face of massive hepatic necrosis, there may be rare cases in which liver enzymes may be normal.
The best indicators of hepatocellular failure are glucose, fibrinogen, and prothrombin time and they should be monitored if hepatic dysfunction is documented.
Amatoxin detection can be performed on a sample of mushroom using hydrochloric acid (the Meixner test).

Radioimmunoassay and high performance liquid chromatography (HPLC) can detect amatoxins in the serum, urine, and emesis fluid. However, these assays are rarely available in most clinical settings. In addition, Amatoxin levels do not correlate with poisoning severity.

Orellanine (Cortinarius) poisoning can be confirmed with plasma assays for orellanine or orelline. High performance liquid chromatography can be used to quantitatively assess psilocybin poisoning. Psilocybin (hallucinogenic) mushrooms can be hepatotoxic. However, they may cause only a minimal rise in aminotransferases.
See for a recommended approach to management of the patient with suspected mushroom poisoning, and for information about specific toxidromes, their symptoms, and treatment.

The administration of activated charcoal as an aqueous slurry is recommended for patients that present early (<1 hour) after significant ingestion of unknown mushrooms who have not yet developed GI symptoms or CNS depression. Administer 25-50 g for adults, 25 g for patients 1-12 years old, or 1 g/kg for infants. After the 50 g dose, give 12.5 g/hr every 4 hours, or 6.25 g/hr for children. Evaluate bowel sounds to monitor for obstruction. Gastric lavage by nasogastric suction should be performed if spontaneous vomiting has not occurred. C

Vigorous fluid rehydration is recommended for all unknown mushroom poisonings. Forced diuresis (i.e., IV fluids with furosemide to promote urine output of >200 mL/hr) is no longer recommended. Recent studies have shown that forced diuresis can worsen acute kidney injury, even precipitating the need for renal transplant (suspected mechanism is concentration of toxins in the kidneys with forced diuresis).

Previously, forced diuresis had been recommended as a potential adjuvant to other treatments, as earlier studies suggested this would enhance elimination rates and theoretically increase toxin clearance. Recent studies have not shown that forced diuresis increases toxin elimination rate.C

For potentially deadly Amanita ingestion, IV penicillin G and silibinin have been traditionally recommended to competitively inhibit amatoxin uptake by hepatocytes. Ongoing studies show that both silibinin and N-acetylcysteine appear to be most efficacious, when administered as soon as possible.C

For Gyromitra ingestion, administer antiemetics, correct fluid deficits and electrolyte derangements. If seizures occur, these should be treated with benzodiazepines and pyridoxine. For refractory seizures, barbituates or propofol may be utilized. C
See and for general and specific treatment of mushroom poisoning. Specific therapy depends on the presumed toxin ingested.
Gastric lavage is performed only if the patient is admitted in the asymptomatic phase and within 6 hours following ingestion.

For unknown mushroom ingestion, activated charcoal as a slurry can be given early in the presentation (30 g charcoal with at least 240 mL water). Usual doses: 25 to 100 g in adults/adolescents, 25 to 50 g in children (ages 1-12), 0.5 to 1.0 g/kg in infants. Multiple doses can be considered in order to prevent re-absorption of toxin in the gut, but this has not been shown to change outcomes.

Most children will do well with no gastrointestinal decontamination in North American "backyard" mushroom ingestions. Decontamination is not necessary in most ingestions, and if used, ipecac is a reasonable option.
Atropine can be given for severe cholinergic/muscarinic symptoms. Adults: atropine 0.5 to 1 mg IV. Children: atropine 0.01 mg/kg.
Benzodiazepines are used for severe anticholinergic symptoms, agitation, or hallucinogenic symptoms. Physostigmine is rarely needed for anticholinergic symptoms.

Nephrotoxicity has been increasingly recognized as a major cause of morbidity. Renal failure can result from dehydration, rhabdomyolysis or hepatorenal syndrome. Additionally, some cases of acute tubular necrosis may be directly caused by amotoxins. In severe cases, this may require hemodialysis, or even renal transplantation.26.

Forced diuresis (i.e., IV fluids with furosemide to promote urine output of >200 mL/hr) is NOT recommended to treat mushroom toxidromes. In the past, forced diuresis had been recommended as a potential adjuvant to other treatments. This had been studied primarily in Amatoxin and Orellanine syndromes, as these toxins are known to be renally cleared and cause nephrotoxity. Increasing diuresis to enhance the elimination rate of toxins should theoretically increase toxin clearance, but recent studies have not shown that this increases toxin elimination rate. In fact, studies suggest that forced diuresis can worsen acute kidney injury by increasing the concentration of Orellanine in the kidney, potentiating cortical damage. Exact mechanism is unknown. Subsequent need for renal transplantation has been reported.

In addition to aggressive rehydration, administer activated charcoal, 25-50 mg for adults, 25 mg for children 1-12 years old, or 1 g/kg for infants. Subsequent doses of 12.5 g/hr for adults, or 6.25 g/hr for infants, may be given every 4 hours. Monitor for signs of bowel obstruction. Consider gastric lavage, if spontaneous vomiting has not occurred, or nasogastric suctioning between charcoal doses. Multiple doses of charcoal may increase elimination, but has not been shown to change outcomes or decrease mortality.

For potentially deadly Amanita ingestion, IV penicillin G and silibinin have been traditionally recommended to competitively inhibit amatoxin uptake by hepatocytes. The use of both IV penicillin and silibinin together was shown in some studies to have no beneficial effect on survival. Ongoing studies show that both silibinin and N-acetylcysteine appear to be most efficacious, when administered as soon as possible.
Giving penicillin G may competitively inhibit amatoxin uptake by hepatocytes. The dose is 300,000-1,000,000 units/day, though preliminary studies fail to show any decrease in mortality..

Initial treatment is a benzodiazepine (diazepam or lorazepam) IV to control seizures and hallucinations. Also administer pyridoxine as soon as possible. This dose is 25 mg/kg IV over 15 to 30 minutes, repeated for recurrent symptoms, up to a maximum of 15 to 20 g. If these are ineffective or unavilable, alternatives are phenobarbital or propofol.

Liver transplant is only definite treatment for fulminant liver failure. Consider transfer to a transplant center for evaluation. This may be considered for patients with stage II or higher hepatic encephalopathy and for patients with hepatorenal syndrome.
For patients whose renal function does not recover with dialysis, renal transplantation may be necessary. 26

Silibinin: Found in silymarin (milk thistle, Silybum marianum), this compound is being studied as an antidote for amatoxin. It may block amatoxin uptake by hepatocytes. If used, the dose is 5 mg/kg IV loading dose, followed by 20 mg/kg/day continuous IV infusion. Available in Europe, this may not be readily available in the United States. It may be obtained as part of an open label clinical trial by calling 866-520-4412
Vigorous fluid rehydration is recommended for all unknown mushroom poisonings.
Agitation: reassurance, benzodiazepines. Adults: diazepam 5 to10 mg by mouth or 0.05 to 0.1 mg/kg IV. Children: diazepam 0.1 to 0.2 mg/kg orally.

Seizures: Adults: diazepam 5 to 10 mg IV OR 0.15 mg/kg IV up to 10 mg per dose up to a rate of 5 mg/min; may be repeated every 5 to 20 minutes as needed. Consider phenobarbital if seizures persist after diazepam greater than 30 mg. Children: diazepam 0.1 to 0.5 mg/kg IV over 2 to 5 minutes; up to a maximum dose of 10 mg/dose. May repeat dose every 5 to 10 minutes as needed. Consider phenobarbital if seizures persist after diazepam 10 mg in children older than 5 years, after diazepam 5 mg in children younger than 5 years.
Refer or hospitalize patients with signs of worsening hepatic or renal function, or progressive toxidrome.
Identifying the time to symptom onset can help determine the mushroom toxidrome, guide medical management, and assist with defining prognosis. C

Longitudinal data from the American Association of Poison Control Centers (1989-1995) suggest that 50% of all patients with mushroom poisoning develop no symptoms and 25% require treatment. On average, 10% to 15% will experience minor toxicity, less than 8% moderate toxicity, and 0.4% major toxicity.

The mortality rate with Amanita mushroom poisoning is 20% to 30%, but can be reduced to less than 5% with appropriate early intensive care. A French study of paitents admitted to the ICU with cyclopeptide poisoning, showed that 6.9% required dialysis and 2.5% ncessitated liver transplantation. 25 C
Toxic hepatitis in the fetus has been reported in amanita poisoning during pregnancy.
Follow adult guidelines with medication dose adjustment.

feature.caption: Approach to Suspected Mushroom Poisoning.
feature.feature_body:
Prehospital management Bring whole mushrooms/pieces to the hospital for identification. Transport samples wrapped in wax paper in a paper bag and refrigerate. Give activated charcoal in the field for potentially toxic mushroom ingestion if patient is awake and is able to protect the airway.a Charcoal is most effective if given within 1 hr of mushroom consumption.
Obtain history and chronology of mushroom ingestion. Establish onset of toxicity: Early (<6 hr): suspect milder toxidrome with less severe course. Late (6-24 hr): suspect severe toxidrome with possible lethal intoxication. Delayed (1 d or more): suspect delayed renal failure, rhabdomyolysis, or neurotoxicity.b
Obtain appropriate laboratory studies. Consider gastric lavage if patient presents within 6 hr of ingestion. Attempt to identify mushroom species ingested. Consider Spore Print: Place mushroom caps on white and black papers, gills down, and cover with a jar. Assess spore color after 2 or more hours. Consider consulting POISINDEX® System electronic guidelines via State Poison Control Center (institutional subscription required).c Consider consulting a mycologist via a State Poison Control Center.
Give supportive care. Give IV fluids: 0.9% NS. Give activated charcoal. Consider repeat doses every 1-4 hr, but not shown to change outcomes. Monitor electrolytes and hepatic profile. Consider benzodiazepines for anxiety/agitation.
Suspect Amanita toxidrome; consider radioimmunoassay to detect amatoxin in serum, urine, or GI fluid. Amatoxin levels do not correlate with poisoning severity. Give IV fluids (D10 ½NS) and monitor electrolytes/glucose hourly. Forced diuresis is no longer recommended. Previous studies on Amatoxin and Orellanine toxidromes suggested that forced diuresis should theoretically increase clearance of the toxin. However, recent studies have not shown that forced diuresis increases toxin elimination rate. Studies have shown that forced diuresis can worsen acute kidney injury (exact mechanism is unknown), resulting in subsequent renal transplantation.c Use oral gastric tube to aspirate mushroom fragments (if within 1 hr of ingestion). Monitor ‡PT, BP, urine output, and liver function tests. Consider fresh frozen plasma/vitamin K for coagulopathy or hemorrhage; silibinin if available via IV infusion; penicillin G via IV infusion. Transfer to liver transplant center if signs of hepatic failure are present.
Watch for: rhabdomyolysis (24-72 hr), CNS toxicity (≥24 hr), and oliguric renal failure (days to weeks later). Consider hemodialysis and protein restriction (40 g daily).
Admit to the hospital if prolonged vomiting, dehydration, seizures, or signs of worsening toxicity are present. Observe until patient is symptom free. Follow-upa: liver function tests 36 hr after exposure. Assess renal function (creatinine) every 24-36 hr for 10-14 d.
Consult subspecialty service early for signs of toxicity. Early transfer to liver/renal transplant center is recommended if signs of worsening toxicity are present.
